analysis.one_liner: Requires carmakers to share vehicle data, repair information, and tools with owners and independent shops.
analysis.headline: The REPAIR Act drew 45 bipartisan cosponsors and cleared a House subcommittee by voice vote in February 2026, but more than a year after introduction it has not received a full committee vote or a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar car and truck makers from using technology or contracts to keep owners, independent repair shops, and aftermarket parts companies from getting the vehicle data, repair procedures, and diagnostic tools needed to fix modern vehicles. Owners would get the same access to data that the manufacturer and its dealers have, including over wireless connections, and could choose any shop or tow provider. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules, and NHTSA would write regulations informing buyers of their rights. The bill would also override state laws covering the same ground.
analysis.who_benefits: Car and truck owners, who would pay market rates for repairs instead of being steered to dealer service centers; independent repair shops, which would get the data and tools to work on newer vehicles; and aftermarket parts and diagnostic tool makers, who could build compatible products.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers may not use technological or legal barriers to stop owners or their chosen shops from accessing vehicle-generated data through the OBD port or wireless telematics, or from getting critical repair information and tools on the same terms as dealers.
Manufacturers cannot require or imply that owners use a particular brand of parts or tools, and cannot limit which people an owner designates to access the vehicle.

The bill voids contract provisions, such as repair waivers, that manufacturers use to get around these rights, and bars offering owners compensation in exchange for waiving the right to choose a repair facility.
Accessed data must be deleted within 72 hours of an owner's request and cannot be sold or used for unrelated purposes, with a de-identified exception only for research and development.

The FTC would enforce the Act as an unfair or deceptive practice, with a complaint process any person can use, and NHTSA must write rules requiring manufacturers to tell buyers their rights at the point of purchase.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers and franchised dealerships, which currently control repair data and tools and capture a large share of post-sale service revenue; they would lose that gatekeeping position and face compliance costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state laws covering the same ground, so states with stronger right-to-repair rules — such as Massachusetts' voter-approved automotive data law — could not enforce tougher requirements than this federal standard.
Vehicles equipped with automated driving systems are excluded from the bill entirely, leaving data and repair access for self-driving technology unregulated as it develops.

Broadening access to vehicle data ports and wireless systems raises security and privacy risks that automakers cite; the bill lets manufacturers keep cryptographic protections for safety-critical systems, but opponents argue any expanded access creates new paths for tampering or data misuse.

A company accused of violating the Act can escape liability for a complaint simply by ceasing the conduct and making reparation within the FTC's timeline, which critics could see as a soft penalty structure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For owners of newer vehicles, the benefit is concrete: repair and maintenance choices at competitive prices instead of dealer-only service. The main design costs are real but narrower — the preemption clause could cap state-level protections at this federal floor, and self-driving vehicles are left out. On balance the bill is a straightforward consumer and small-business competition measure, though its enforcement penalties are relatively gentle on manufacturers that comply after a complaint.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee by voice vote in February 2026, but the full committee has never voted on it and it has not reached the House floor; it dies unless the committee and floor act before this Congress ends in January 2027.

narrative.text: Rep. Neal Dunn introduced the REPAIR Act on February 25, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and then to its Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade Subcommittee.
The bill gathered 45 cosponsors, split nearly evenly between 23 Democrats and 22 Republicans.
On February 10, 2026, the subcommittee held a consideration and markup session and forwarded the bill to the full committee by voice vote.
No further action has been taken; the full committee has not scheduled a markup and the House has not voted on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and dealership service centers, which keep control of vehicle data, repair information, and post-sale service revenue while the bill sits without a full committee vote. Car owners and independent shops continue to face manufacturer-controlled access to data and repairs.

for.name: Rep. Neal Dunn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled a bipartisan group of 15 original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 45 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on across party lines, giving the bill one of the more balanced bipartisan bases of any House bill this Congress.

for.name: Automotive aftermarket industry (Auto Care Association and allied repair, parts, and tool companies)
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned for the bill as the lead outside supporter of automotive right-to-repair legislation.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (Chair Brett Guthrie)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill at subcommittee level; after the subcommittee forwarded it on February 10, 2026, the full committee never scheduled a markup or vote.

against.name: Alliance for Automotive Innovation (automaker trade group)
against.what_they_did: Opposed right-to-repair mandates on security, safety, and data-control grounds.

sides.party_line_note: Support splits almost evenly across parties — 23 Democratic and 22 Republican cosponsors with a Republican sponsor — and the subcommittee forwarded the bill on a voice vote; the obstacle is committee inaction, not party opposition on the record.

industries.note: The bill ends their gatekeeping over vehicle data, repair information, and tools, which underpins high-margin dealer service work and control of the aftermarket. They keep cryptographic protections for safety-critical systems but lose the legal and technical barriers the bill prohibits.

Shops would get the same data and tools as dealers, letting them service newer vehicles — including wireless-diagnosed repairs — that many currently cannot. One of their number also holds a seat on the bill's advisory committee.

industries.industry: Aftermarket parts and diagnostic tool manufacturers
industries.note: The bill bars manufacturers from blocking compatible aftermarket parts and from mandating brand-name parts, opening the replacement-parts and tool markets to competition.
Dealers currently capture repair work steered to them by data and tool access; equal access for independents would put that revenue at risk. They also get an advisory committee seat.
They hold advisory committee seats and benefit from competitive repair costs, but have no direct obligation under the bill.

analysis.trajectory: Bills at this stage — favorably reported by subcommittee but waiting over a year for full-committee action — rarely reach the floor unless leadership prioritizes them, and similar right-to-repair bills have stalled in prior Congresses despite bipartisan cosponsors. With no full-committee markup scheduled and limited floor time left before January 2027, the likeliest path is that the bill dies in committee again, though a late committee markup and suspension vote remain possible given the bipartisan base.
